payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
Two producers each hold a verified signature over the same track. Both records check out completely: right keys, untampered content, independent timestamps, nothing forged anywhere. Each names a different sole author of the same master, and the claims cannot both be true. Anyone expecting the mathematics to break the tie will wait forever. Verification will keep confirming both records until the algorithms themselves retire, and the system is not malfunctioning. It was never built to hold a trial.

A valid signature proves attribution, not truth

A signature that verifies establishes that a specific key produced it over exactly this content, and an anchored one adds that the record existed no later than a known moment. The truth of the sentence being signed was never an input to any of it. This is the smaller promise a signature makes: attribution rather than truth, an author bound to a claim rather than a claim certified as fact. Two authors bound to incompatible claims was therefore always going to happen, and the design treats it as an ordinary human situation. People disagree about who made what, and now they disagree in writing, under their own names.

In a royalty dispute a verified signature is the end of the conversation, and that holds where one signed record meets an unsigned assertion. A second signed record is the open case. The conversation resumes, and what follows is worth walking through, because the conflict that resumes is a much smaller one.

The geometry of the collision

Start with what the collision fixes in place. Nobody is disputing an anonymous metadata row.

What a collision fixes in place

Names. Both claimants are named. Each claim carries a key, and each key an accountable identity.

Order. Anchored timestamps cannot be backdated, so whichever claim came second came second permanently.

Stakes. Whichever record loses, its signer owns it forever.

The sequence does not decide the truth, because an honest party can easily sign later than a liar, but it removes an entire genre of argument: nobody can manufacture an earlier claim after learning they need one.

The dispute has changed shape. Before signatures it was an open question about the world, reconstructed from session invoices and whoever's memory survived. Now it is a closed question about two named people, one of whom has signed a false statement with an instrument built to make statements permanent. False testimony has existed as long as testimony. False testimony that can never be withdrawn or reassigned to a database error is new.

The verdict stays human

No protocol picks the winner, and proposals to add one deserve suspicion, since any mechanism that can overrule a valid signature is a mechanism for taking work away from authors wholesale. Adjudication stays where it has always been, with people. What the record changes is what arrives in front of them: two sealed claims, a fixed sequence, named parties, and stakes that were set the moment each side signed.

The economics run in the honest direction. Signing a false authorship claim was always possible, and what changed is the price, which is now a permanent, attributable, dated act of fraud that any future dispute can retrieve. Most lies prefer cheaper instruments. A signed collision will usually mean one party miscalculated badly, which is exactly the kind of event courts are good at pricing, and it should stay rare for the same reason signed contracts are breached less often than handshakes.

What has no answer yet is the forum. Every existing venue for authorship disputes, from collecting society committees to courtrooms, is built for evidence scarcity, for reconstructing what nobody wrote down. Two perfect, contradictory records hand those venues the opposite problem, an evidence surplus with no procedure attached, and nobody has written the rules for that yet.
payload.title: Two valid signatures can disagree
